title: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
summary: Write performance pull requests reviewers can trust: tune and order runs to cut noise and bias, test significance with t and U tests, report geomeans and costs honestly, and read CI regression thresholds.
outcomes: Explain what evidence a performance PR needs and why one before and after number is not enough
Distinguish noise from bias and design run order and setup to control both
Compute a t score and interpret t-test and Mann-Whitney U results from pyperf, compare.py and benchstat
Summarize a suite with a geometric mean and explain why rerunning until significant is an error
Compute an IQR-based regression threshold as rustc-perf does and decide which changes are significant

lessons.title: What a reviewer needs before merging a speedup

blocks.md:
A performance pull request asks a maintainer to accept new code, often more complex code, in exchange for a claimed gain in speed or memory. The diff alone cannot show that gain. The reviewer has to trust your measurement, so the measurement is the real content of the PR.

The Linux kernel's patch guide says it directly: "Quantify optimizations and trade-offs. If you claim improvements in performance, memory consumption, stack footprint, or binary size, include numbers that back them up." It then asks you to "describe non-obvious costs", because optimizations usually trade CPU against memory and readability, or one workload against another.

Other projects say the same in their own way. Go's [contribution guide](https://go.dev/doc/contribute) asks for benchmark data when a change affects performance and notes that the `benchstat` tool is conventionally used to format it. The Rust compiler guide says a reviewer may request a "perf run", a benchmark of the whole compiler on a collection of popular crates, before approving a change that might affect performance.

Why is "it took 120 ms before and 100 ms after" not enough? A single run of each side cannot separate your change from run-to-run **noise** (random variation from the CPU, OS and caches). It also says nothing about **bias** (a systematic difference in setup that favors one side), whether the workload matters to users, or what the change costs. From the microbenchmarking prerequisite, recall that a benchmark can also measure the wrong thing entirely (dead code removed by the compiler, cold caches, no warmup); a good PR shows it was checked.

blocks.title: The evidence chain behind a performance claim

nodes.label:
Costs: memory, size,
complexity, other workloads

Reviewer reruns
or requests a perf run

scenes.caption: Two artifacts that differ only by your change: the exact baseline commit and your patched commit. Anything else that differs (compiler, flags, machine) becomes part of the result.
Both are measured with the same benchmark on the same machine, many times each. Repetition is what lets a tool separate a real change from noise.
A comparison tool turns the two sets of samples into a relative change plus a significance verdict, instead of you eyeballing two numbers.
The PR carries the numbers and the costs the kernel guide asks for: what got bigger, slower or harder to read, and which workloads may lose.
Because the setup and commands are written down, a reviewer can rerun them, or trigger the project's own benchmark bot, and check for regressions.

blocks.md:
A complete performance claim has five parts:

1. **Workload**: what you ran and why it represents real use.
2. **Setup**: hardware, OS, compiler and flags, and any system tuning.
3. **Method**: how many runs, in what order, with which tool.
4. **Results**: before, after, the spread, and whether the difference is significant.
5. **Costs**: memory, binary size, complexity, and workloads that may get slower.

blocks.code:
encoding/json: avoid reflect lookup in Encode hot path

Encoding a small struct spent most of its time looking up
field metadata on every call. Cache it per type.

Measured with go test -bench=Encode -count=10 on an idle
linux/amd64 machine, before and after runs interleaved.

                      | old.txt     | new.txt                       |
                      | sec/op      | sec/op     vs base            |
Encode/format=json-48   1.718u +- 1%  1.423u +- 1% -17.20% (p=0.000 n=10)
Encode/format=gob-48    3.066u +- 0%  3.070u +- 2%       ~ (p=0.446 n=10)
geomean                 2.295u        2.090u        -8.94%

Cost: one cache entry per encoded type (grows with the
number of distinct types, never freed).
blocks.caption: Illustrative commit message in Go's style. The benchmark table is the example output from the benchstat documentation (box characters and the micro sign replaced with ASCII); the change and cost text are invented for the example.

blocks.md: A performance claim is an experiment. The PR must let a reviewer rerun it (exact commands, setup, commits) and weigh it (spread, significance and costs), not just read a headline number.

Common misconception: "the new number is smaller, so the change is faster". Two single measurements differ almost always, even for identical code. Without repeated runs and a test, a 5% gap can be pure noise.

blocks.question: Which PR description gives a reviewer the most to act on?
options: "About 20% faster on my machine."
"Encode is 17.2% faster (median of 10 interleaved runs each, p=0.000 via benchstat, idle linux/amd64); cache adds one entry per type."
"Encode is much faster now; see the flame graph screenshot."
"Benchmarks pass in CI, so performance is fine."
blocks.explain: Only the second states the method (10 interleaved runs, median), a significance result, the setup, and the cost. The others give no way to judge noise or to rerun the experiment, and "CI passes" usually checks correctness, not speed.

blocks.question: Besides numbers that back up a claimed gain, what else does the kernel's patch guide ask for in an optimization patch?
options: A link to a third-party benchmark website
Proof that the gain holds on every architecture Linux supports
A description of the non-obvious costs and expected downsides, so the reviewer can weigh them
Nothing else: numbers alone are sufficient
blocks.explain: The guide says optimizations usually trade CPU, memory and readability, or one workload against another, and asks you to describe the expected downsides so the reviewer can weigh costs against benefits.

lessons.title: Noise and bias: making before and after comparable

blocks.md: Two different things can make a benchmark lie. **Noise** is random variation: the same binary gives 100.2 ms, then 99.7 ms, then 101.1 ms. Repeating runs and averaging shrinks its effect. **Bias** is systematic: something about the setup favors one side every time. Repetition does nothing against bias. LLVM's benchmarking tips put it this way: low noise "is required, but not sufficient. It does not exclude measurement bias."

Google Benchmark's variance guide lists common noise sources:

- CPU frequency scaling, and boost features (Turbo Boost, Precision Boost) that change the clock even under the "performance" governor
- running on a different core from one run to the next
- context switches and competing processes on the same CPU
- SMT (Hyper-Threading) siblings sharing a core, and cache effects from other CPUs
- NUMA (memory attached to different CPU sockets)

blocks.code:
# pyperf: tune the machine (Linux, needs root), and undo it afterwards
python3 -m pyperf system tune
python3 -m pyperf system reset

# Or do the main steps by hand
sudo cpupower frequency-set --governor performance
echo 0 | sudo tee /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/boost   # disable boost
taskset -c 2 ./mybenchmark                                # pin to one CPU

# Whole commands: hyperfine runs warmups, then at least 10 timed runs
hyperfine --warmup 3 './tool-old input.txt' './tool-new input.txt'
blocks.caption: Commands from the pyperf, Google Benchmark and hyperfine docs. The boost file path depends on the CPU frequency driver.

blocks.md: `pyperf system tune` bundles several of these: it sets the CPU scaling governor to `performance`, raises the minimum CPU frequency to the maximum, stops the `irqbalance` service and moves interrupt affinity, lowers the perf-event sample rate, and disables Intel Turbo Boost where it can. It also checks whether CPUs are isolated with the `isolcpus=` kernel option. The pyperf docs report that isolating at least one core has a significant impact on stability, and LLVM's guide says that with shielded cores, SMT siblings disabled and `perf stat -r 10`, you can expect variations under 0.1%.

blocks.prompt: No code changed: A and B are the same binary, true time 100 ms. But the machine slowly heats up, so each run slot takes 0.4 ms (0.4% of the true time) longer than the previous one. You run 6 runs of A, then 6 runs of B. What does the comparison report?
blocks.reveal: B looks **2.38% slower** (mean 103.4 ms vs 101.0 ms), and with this little noise a test would call it significant. The drift is bias: every B run happened later than every A run. Repeating more runs in the same order makes the false result *more* confident, not less.

blocks.title: Run order turns drift into a fake regression

scenes.caption: Blocked order: all A runs, then all B runs. Labels are each run's time in ms under the drift model. Mean A is 101.0, mean B is 103.4: B looks 2.38% slower with no code change.
Interleaved A, B, A, B: drift now lands on both sides. Mean A 102.0, mean B 102.4. The fake gap shrinks to 0.39%, because B still always runs one slot after A.

A, B, B, A pattern: under a linear drift each pair of slots balances out exactly. Both means are 102.2 ms and the fake gap is 0.00%. Simplified: real drift is not linear, so randomizing order also helps.

blocks.title: Apparent B vs A slowdown from drift alone

scenes.caption: Blocked order reports a 2.38% regression that does not exist.
Interleaving cuts the bias to 0.39%; benchstat's docs recommend interleaving before and after runs for exactly this reason.
Balancing the order removes linear drift completely in this model (0.00%).

blocks.md: Bias also hides in places you would never suspect. Mytkowicz and colleagues ([ASPLOS 2009](https://users.cs.northwestern.edu/~robby/courses/322-2013-spring/mytkowicz-wrong-data.pdf)) measured the speedup of gcc's `-O3` over `-O2` while changing only the **link order** of object files or the **size of the UNIX environment** (an unused environment variable), both of which shift code and stack layout. For perlbench on a Core 2, link order alone moved the measured speedup between 0.92 (O3 slower) and 1.10 (O3 faster). For lbm, environment size moved it between 0.88 and 1.09.

blocks.title: Same code, different layout: measured O3 speedup

scenes.caption: perlbench, 33 builds that differ only in link order: the measured O3 speedup ranged from 0.92 to 1.10. Values below 1.0 mean O3 looked slower.
lbm, changing only the size of the environment: 0.88 to 1.09. A layout accident can be larger than the effect a typical PR claims.

blocks.md: A small, very stable difference can still be a layout accident: your patch moved code, and alignment changed. If a 1 to 2% win appears in code you did not expect to matter, rebuild with a different layout (the paper calls this setup randomization) or test on another machine before claiming it.
Repetition fights noise; only experimental design fights bias. Same machine, same build flags, interleaved or balanced run order, and a second setup for surprising results.

blocks.question: After `pyperf system tune` and CPU pinning, your runs vary by only 0.1%, and the patched build is 1.5% faster in every run. What can you still not conclude?
options: That the result is affected by noise
That the 1.5% comes from your change rather than a layout or order effect that favors the patched build
That the benchmark ran at all
That pyperf was installed correctly
blocks.explain: Low noise makes the gap statistically clear, but it says nothing about bias. Run order, code layout or environment size can shift one build consistently. Interleaving, rebuilding with different layouts or another machine tests for that.

blocks.question: Why does benchstat's documentation recommend interleaving before and after runs?
options: It makes each individual run faster
Go benchmarks crash when run in blocks
So that slow changes in the machine (heat, background jobs) hit both versions evenly instead of only one
Because the U test requires alternating samples
blocks.explain: Noise must be spread evenly across both versions. In blocked order, any drift during the session is attributed entirely to whichever version ran later.

lessons.title: Is the difference real? t-tests, U tests and p-values

blocks.md: With repeated runs you have two samples: n times before and n times after. The question is whether the gap between them is larger than the noise inside each sample. Statistics frames it as a **null hypothesis**: "the change made no difference". A test computes a **p-value**, the probability of seeing a gap at least this large if the null hypothesis were true. If p is below a threshold **alpha** (0.05 by default in benchstat and Google Benchmark's compare.py), the difference is called statistically significant.

pyperf's `compare_to` uses Student's two-sample, two-tailed t-test at the 95% level. Its source computes a t score from the two means and the **pooled variance** (the spread of both samples combined), then compares it with a **critical value**: the score that pure noise exceeds only 5% of the time, read from the t distribution for $2n-2$ **degrees of freedom** (the number of runs minus the two means estimated from them). If $|t|$ is at least the critical value, it reports the change; otherwise it prints "Not significant!".

blocks.tex: t = \frac{\bar a - \bar b}{\sqrt{2 s_p^2 / n}}, \qquad s_p^2 = \frac{\sum_i (a_i - \bar a)^2 + \sum_i (b_i - \bar b)^2}{2n - 2}
blocks.caption: pyperf's t score for two samples of equal size n. For n = 5 per side, df = 8 and the 95% critical value is 2.306.

blocks.prompt: Experiment 1: baseline mean 100 ms, patched mean 97 ms (a 3 ms gap). Experiment 2: baseline 100 ms, patched 96 ms (a 4 ms gap). Both use 5 runs per side. Which one does pyperf call significant?
blocks.reveal: Only **experiment 1**. Its runs barely vary (pooled variance 2.5, so t = 3.0, above 2.306). Experiment 2 has the bigger gap but its runs swing by several ms (pooled variance 18, t = 1.49), so the gap is within the noise. Significance depends on gap divided by spread, not on the gap alone.

blocks.title: Worked t-test: same size gap, different noise

scenes.caption: Experiment 1. Baseline runs stay within 2 ms of their mean (100), patched runs within 2 ms of theirs (97). Pooled variance is 2.5.
t = 3 / sqrt(2 x 2.5 / 5) = 3.00. That is above the critical value 2.306 for df = 8, so pyperf reports the change as significant.
Experiment 2. The gap is larger (100 vs 96) but runs swing by up to 6 ms. Pooled variance is 18.
t = 4 / sqrt(2 x 18 / 5) = 1.49, below 2.306: "Not significant!". The answer is more runs or less noise, not a bigger headline number.

blocks.md: The t-test compares means and works best when samples are roughly bell-shaped. benchstat and Google Benchmark's `compare.py` instead use the **Mann-Whitney U test**, a non-parametric test (it makes no assumption about the shape of the distribution). It looks only at order: across every pair of one before-run and one after-run, how often is the before-run slower? With 10 runs per side there are 100 pairs. If nothing changed you expect about half, 50; if every pair favors the new code, U is 100. benchstat also summarizes each side with the **median** and a 95% confidence interval instead of the mean.

blocks.title: U test on benchstat's example data (ns/op, sorted)

scenes.caption: Encode/format=json, 10 runs each from the benchstat docs. With 10 values the median is the average of the 5th and 6th (marked): 1718 and 1422.5 ns, a change of -17.20%.
Every new value (max 1447) is below every old value (min 1705): all 100 pairs favor new, so U = 100. benchstat prints p=0.000.
Encode/format=gob: the samples overlap. Old is slower in only 39.5 of 100 pairs (ties count half), close to the 50 expected with no change. benchstat prints "~" with p=0.446.

blocks.md: Recomputing with SciPy's `mannwhitneyu` on the same data gives U = 100 for json (exact p about 0.00001 with `method='exact'`; SciPy's default normal approximation gives about 0.0002) and U = 39.5 with p of about 0.45 for gob, in line with benchstat's printed values. In Google Benchmark, run with `--benchmark_repetitions=N` so `compare.py` has samples; it reports changes as $(new - old)/|old|$ and its docs warn the U test needs no fewer than 9 repetitions to be meaningful.

How many runs do you need? For the t-test, the score grows with $\sqrt{n}$. Writing the true change as $\delta$ and the noise as the coefficient of variation CV (standard deviation divided by mean), both in percent, the score is about $\delta / (CV\sqrt{2/n})$. Drag the sliders below: with a 1% change and 2% CV, you need 32 runs per side to reach the critical value of about 2.0; halve the noise to 1% CV and 9 runs suffice.

blocks.title: t score vs runs per side

scenes.caption: 1% change, 2% CV: t reaches 2.0 only at 32 runs per side. With 10 runs, t is 1.12 and the change would be missed.
Halve the noise to 1% CV: t reaches the critical value at 9 runs (2.121 vs 2.120 for df 16). Halving noise cuts the runs needed by about 4x.
A 5% change at 2% CV is clear with 3 runs per side. Big wins are easy to show; small ones need tuning or many runs.

blocks.md: Significant is not the same as large. benchstat's docs stress that with enough low-noise data even very small changes become significant. Report the size of the change and its spread, and use the test only to answer "is this more than noise?"

blocks.question: You run Google Benchmark's compare.py with 3 repetitions per side. The time column shows -0.04 (4% faster) and the p-value is 0.10. What is the right conclusion?
options: The change makes it 4% faster; p-values above 0.05 only matter for regressions
There is not enough evidence either way: rerun with at least 9 repetitions, decided in advance
The change has no effect, since the test failed
The change is 10% likely to be faster
blocks.explain: Failing to reject the null hypothesis is not proof of no effect, especially with 3 samples; the tool's docs warn the U test needs no fewer than 9 repetitions. With 3 runs per side the smallest p the two-sided U test can give is 0.10, so it could never pass 0.05. Choose a sample size up front and rerun once, rather than reading the 4% as either real or zero.

blocks.question: Your benchmark's noise CV drops from 2% to 1% after CPU pinning. Roughly how does the number of runs needed to detect the same change scale?
options: It halves
It stays the same
It drops to about a quarter
It doubles
blocks.explain: Runs needed scale with the square of noise over effect: n is about 2 (t CV / delta) squared. Halving CV cuts n by about 4, from 32 to 9 runs per side for a 1% change in the worked model.

lessons.title: Reporting honestly: geomeans, many benchmarks and costs

blocks.md: Real projects run a suite of benchmarks, and a change speeds some up and slows others down. Both pyperf and benchstat summarize a suite with the **geometric mean** of the per-benchmark ratios (new over old). pyperf's docs cite Fleming and Wallace's 1986 paper on summarizing benchmark results for this choice. A geometric mean treats a 2x slowdown and a 2x speedup as cancelling, which an arithmetic mean of ratios does not.

blocks.caption: A value below 1 means faster overall. If one of k benchmarks doubles in time, the geomean grows by a factor of the k-th root of 2 (1.072 for k = 10).

blocks.title: pyperf docs example: Python 3.7 vs 3.6 (time ratio)

scenes.caption: Per-benchmark time ratios from the pyperf compare_to example: 2.09/2.13 = 0.981 (faster), 5.28/3.70 = 1.427 and 6.05/4.61 = 1.312 (slower).
Geometric mean of the three: 1.225, printed as 1.22x slower. One benchmark improved, but the suite as a whole regressed, and the summary says so.

blocks.md: The same applies to benchstat's example: json went from 1.718 to 1.423 µs (-17.20%) and gob did not change significantly (3.066 vs 3.070 µs). The geomean of medians goes from 2.295 to 2.090 µs, a -8.94% change. A PR that quoted only "17% faster" without the per-benchmark table would oversell it.

blocks.prompt: Your PR touches nothing that matters for speed. You run 20 independent benchmarks and test each at alpha = 0.05. What is the probability that at least one is reported as a significant change?
blocks.reveal: About **64%**: $1 - 0.95^{20} = 0.642$. benchstat's docs warn about exactly this: at alpha 0.05 you should *expect* about 5% of benchmarks to show a significant change when nothing changed. One flagged benchmark out of twenty is weak evidence.

blocks.title: Chance of at least one false 'significant' result

scenes.caption: One benchmark, one test: a 5% chance of a false positive, which is what alpha = 0.05 means.
Each extra test is another chance: 22.6% at 5 tests, 40.1% at 10, 64.2% at 20 (computed as 1 - 0.95^k, assuming independent tests).
A 50-benchmark suite almost always flags something by chance (92.3%), and 100 benchmarks 99.4%. Expect noise hits; look for patterns and large effects.

blocks.md: The same trap appears over time: rerunning until the tool finally says "significant" is multiple testing in disguise, and benchstat's docs call it a common statistical error. Their advice: pick a number of runs (at least 10, ideally 20), stick to it, and accept the answer. Report every benchmark in the suite, including the ones that got slower, not just the winners.

Time is not the only cost. Report memory use, binary size and compile time when your change can affect them. For metrics that have no noise, such as the size of a compiled binary, benchstat supports `assume=exact` unit metadata: it then warns about any variation and compares even a single before and after value. And as the kernel guide says, name the trade-off in plain words: more memory for less CPU, a heuristic that helps one workload and hurts another, or code that is harder to read.

blocks.code:
## Performance
Workload: go test -run='^$' -bench=Encode -count=10 (old.txt, new.txt)
Machine: idle linux/amd64, performance governor, runs interleaved
Tool: benchstat old.txt new.txt

<full benchstat table, every benchmark in the package>

## Costs
- Memory: one cache entry per distinct type, never freed
- Code: adds a sync.Map and an invalidation path
- Not improved: gob encoding (~, p=0.446)
blocks.caption: A sketch of a performance section for a PR body: method first, the full table, then the costs. Adapt the commands to your project's own benchmark harness.

blocks.md: Do not cherry-pick. Quoting only the best benchmark, dropping a regressed one, or rerunning until a borderline result flips are all ways to make noise look like a win. Reviewers who rerun your commands will find out.

blocks.question: A suite has 3 benchmarks with time ratios (new/old) 0.50, 2.00 and 1.00. What does the geometric mean say, and what would the arithmetic mean of ratios say?
options: Geomean 1.00 (no change); arithmetic mean 1.17 (17% slower)
Geomean 1.17; arithmetic mean 1.00
Both say 1.00
Geomean 0.50; arithmetic mean 2.00
blocks.explain: The product 0.5 x 2 x 1 = 1, so the geomean is 1.00: a halving and a doubling cancel. The arithmetic mean (0.5 + 2 + 1)/3 = 1.17 is pulled up by the slowdown, which is why suite summaries use the geometric mean of ratios.

blocks.question: Spot the bug in this workflow: "I ran benchstat with -count=10. Result: ~ (p=0.12). I reran twice more; the third time it said -3.1% (p=0.03), so I put that in the PR."
options: Nothing is wrong: the last run is the most recent data
-count=10 is too many runs
It is multiple testing: rerunning until p drops below 0.05 makes a false positive likely, so the reported result is biased
benchstat cannot handle p-values above 0.1
blocks.explain: Each rerun is another chance for noise to cross the threshold. benchstat's docs say to fix the number of runs in advance and not rerun until it reports a change, because that creates a statistical bias toward false positives.

lessons.title: Regression checks: perf bots and noise thresholds from history

blocks.md: Large projects do not rely only on the contributor's laptop. The Rust compiler runs a benchmark suite after every merged PR, tracks results over time on perf.rust-lang.org, and notes changes in a comment on the PR. Before merging, anyone with permission can request a perf run on a PR by commenting `@bors try @rust-timer queue`. The dev guide says to request one if your PR may affect performance, especially adversely, and to ask the reviewer or Zulip if you lack permission.

blocks.title: A Rust perf run on a pull request

scenes.caption: The contributor opens a PR that may change compiler performance and asks for a perf run, since only authorized teams can trigger it.
The reviewer comments the trigger. bors first does a try build: a full release build for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.
When the build finishes, it is queued to run the benchmark suite, compiling a collection of popular crates in several configurations (fresh and incremental builds, among others).
rust-timer posts a summary comment on the PR with a link to the full comparison report against the parent commit.
After merge the suite runs again automatically, so a regression missed before merge still shows up and is noted on the PR.

blocks.md: A bot comparing two commits has one problem a human with benchstat does not: it may have only one measurement per commit per benchmark. rustc-perf solves this with history. For each benchmark it takes the results of the previous 30 commits on the main branch, computes the absolute relative change between each adjacent pair, and treats that spread as the benchmark's normal noise. A new change is **significant** only if it is an outlier against that history, using an interquartile range (IQR) fence.

blocks.caption: Q1 and Q3 are the lower and upper quartiles of historical adjacent-commit changes. With too little history, rustc-perf falls back to a fixed 0.2% threshold.

blocks.title: Learning a noise threshold from history (% change)

scenes.caption: Simplified: 11 commit-to-commit changes of one benchmark (rustc-perf uses 30 commits), sorted. All are under 0.2%: this benchmark is quiet.
Q1 is the median of the lower half (indices 0 to 4): 0.080. Q3 is the median of the upper half (indices 6 to 10): 0.150. IQR = 0.070.
Threshold = 0.150 + 3 x 0.070 = 0.36%. Changes smaller than this are treated as normal noise for this benchmark.
New PR results: +0.20% is below 0.36%, not significant. +0.70% is a significant regression (1.9x the threshold). -0.90% is a significant improvement (2.5x).

blocks.md: How much a change matters also depends on the metric. rustc-perf treats user-space instruction counts as not typically noisy and every other metric (such as wall time or peak memory) as noisy, halving the magnitude it assigns to a given percentage change on noisy metrics. Results are then summarized per PR: if there are both improvements and regressions of medium magnitude or more, the PR is labeled **mixed**, and a human triages it. Other ecosystems follow the same pattern with their own tools; read your project's contributing docs for its benchmark command and bot.

Before opening a performance PR, find the project's own harness (pyperformance for CPython, `go test -bench` plus benchstat for Go, rustc-perf for rustc, a Google Benchmark target for many C++ projects). Numbers from the project's suite are more convincing than a custom script, and reviewers already know how to read them.

Regression checks only work if noise is known. A bot learns each benchmark's normal spread from history and flags changes beyond it; you do the same by hand with repeated, interleaved runs and a test.

blocks.question: A benchmark's historical adjacent-commit changes have Q1 = 0.10% and Q3 = 0.30%. Your PR changes it by +0.75%. Does rustc-perf's rule flag it?
options: Yes: 0.75% is above Q3
No: the threshold is 0.30 + 3 x 0.20 = 0.90%, and 0.75% is below it
Yes: anything above the fixed 0.2% default is flagged
No: only improvements are tested
blocks.explain: The fence is Q3 plus 3 times the IQR: 0.30 + 3 x 0.20 = 0.90%. A 0.75% change is within the benchmark's historical noise. The 0.2% default only applies when there is not enough history.

blocks.question: The perf bot reports your PR as mixed: a target benchmark is 4% faster, but an unrelated one regressed by 1.2%, well above its threshold. What should you do?
options: Ignore it: the bot is noisy
Rerun the bot until the regression disappears
Remove the regressed benchmark from the suite
Investigate the regression and explain the trade-off (or fix it) in the PR so the reviewer can weigh it
blocks.explain: A change beyond the noise threshold is a real signal to investigate. The kernel guide's rule applies: describe the downsides so the reviewer can weigh costs against benefits. Rerunning until it vanishes is multiple testing, and editing the suite hides evidence.
